title: Routines: before a lesson and after a task
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino describes the routines she uses so lesson time is productive at the start, when a task finishes and when students finish early. At the start, students open their booklets and answer review questions silently from memory while she sets up the room, with paired quizzing or a read-then-quiz for low-confidence classes as fallbacks. To tell when work is finished while she cannot circulate, students raise a hand holding a pen, kept distinct from a question hand. She reminds students of the success criteria before independent practice and uses mini whiteboards to model and check that they follow instructions. Early finishers either think back by self-quizzing or look forward by reading ahead. The post is practical and openly a work in progress, grounded in her own pandemic-era classroom rather than research.
points: A fixed entry routine of silent retrieval from memory fills the setup time that distancing and remote learning created.
The pen-in-hand signal separates task completion from questions and gives a quick read on the whole class.
Stating the expected steps, modelling them and rehearsing them on mini whiteboards sets up independent practice to be done correctly.
Early finishers have a named choice, think back or look forward, which prevents wasted learning time.
Routines are described as something to train and refine, with the aim of freeing the teacher to focus on teaching well.
quotes: Effective routines make great classroom teaching possible. I have previously written about general routines that can transform the classroom culture and atmosphere for the better, when executed consistently. In this post, I will share routines for students before they start the lesson and after they finish a task.

As I enter a classroom, students know to be ready by opening their booklets and exercise books. I remind them of the topic and page number we are on for that lesson and they then know to write the title of the section down and answer the review questions in silence and from memory.

When students complete their work, they raise their hand and place it back down again. This tells me very quickly if most students have finished a task. To distinguish this action with a raised hand for a question, I instruct students to hold a pen to signal task completion and to leave their hand empty when raising their hand to ask a question.

This is something that requires training to ensure students know exactly what you expect of them. I always model how I expect students to answer a type of question and I ask them to practice on mini-whiteboards before they work on similar questions independently. The beauty of mini-whiteboards is that I can quickly check if all students are following instructions correctly and if not, I can support them and re-model if necessary.

As students work through questions, inevitably some will finish earlier than others. In these cases, students either sit while waiting for their peers to finish (wasted learning time) or they answer more questions from the booklet that I may have planned for them to complete in a future lesson.

I tell my students to either ‘Think back’ or ‘Look Forward’. When they ‘think back’, students self-quiz using the core questions for the topic we are working on or redo questions they didn’t get right the first time in a previous lesson.
I am still developing these routines but there is no doubt they have made life easier. This means I can focus on teaching well and students know what to expect at each stage of the lesson.
